title: A decision tree, growing
sub: Each split is a yes/no question on one feature, which cuts a box into two.

frames.caption: 90 points, two classes. A decision tree asks yes/no questions about one feature at a time. Start with everything in one box: Gini impurity 0.480.

Split 1: of every possible question, “feature 1 ≤ 4.87?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.480 → 0.297 weighted). CART tried both features at every threshold between data points and kept the best.
Split 2: of every possible question, “feature 2 ≤ 2.77?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.423 → 0.238 weighted).
Split 3: of every possible question, “feature 2 ≤ 1.49?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.476 → 0.346 weighted).
Split 4: of every possible question, “feature 1 ≤ 6.59?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.473 → 0.137 weighted).
Split 5: of every possible question, “feature 1 ≤ 3.98?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.165 → 0.121 weighted).
Split 6: of every possible question, “feature 2 ≤ 2.78?” lowers impurity the most in this box (now split into the two brighter ones) (Gini 0.444 → 0.222 weighted).

Six questions, seven boxes, each labelled by its majority (shading). Keep splitting and the tree will eventually carve out tiny boxes around the noisy points too: 100%% training accuracy, worse on new data. That is why trees are pruned or depth-limited.
